investigations.question: Does the drifted accepted index reach the trim decision? The leader derives its trim index from the minimum of the accepted indexes it has recorded for the configuration's nodes, and those recorded values are exactly the ones the re-synchronization inflates; the documented contract instead requires that all nodes have decided the trim index. Does a drifted minimum let trim remove entries that a replica has not decided, or push the compacted index past the entries a replica still holds?
investigations.hypothesis: Once every node's recorded accepted index is inflated above its content, the minimum the leader uses exceeds the cluster's true minimum content index, so trim can accept a trim index that some replica has not decided (against the documented requirement) and can push the compacted index past that replica's entries; a later re-synchronization of such a replica would then ask the storage for a suffix starting below the compacted index, which the in-memory storage computes by subtracting the compacted index and would underflow.
investigations.discriminator: Sampling, after several reconnection rounds and a leader change so that every node's recorded accepted index exceeds its content, the leader's trim result together with the compacted index it reports and the state of a replica that has not decided that index; the decisive observations are whether trim succeeds beyond the true minimum decided index and whether any later read or re-synchronization of the affected replica panics or silently returns nothing.

interpretations.rationale: Source reading of the re-synchronization path (PrepareReq -> Prepare -> Promise -> AcceptSync -> Accepted) suggests that a replica which has accepted the StopSign gets its accepted index inflated by one when it is re-synchronized at the same ballot: in handle_promise_accept the leader calls send_accsync, whose first branch uses the follower's own accepted index as the valid prefix (leader.rs 150-191), and that index already includes the StopSign because set_stopsign adds it (internal_storage.rs 503-512). create_log_sync then reports that index as LogSync.sync_idx with the sender's StopSign attached, and sync_log adds the StopSign once more, so the follower's accepted index ends at prefix + suffix + 1 while its decided index is the AcceptSync's decided index (internal_storage.rs 313-360). The follower then reports that inflated index in Accepted (follower.rs 112-126), and the leader's decision rule accepts any incoming accepted index whose count reaches a write quorum (leader.rs 316-345), so a write quorum of inflated reports would set the leader's decided index past the entries it holds. Both endpoints this reading endangers are public: is_reconfigured() is gated on stopsign_is_decided() (mod.rs 284-290, state_cache.rs 123-126), the bool of LogEntry::StopSign is documented as 'the reconfiguration has been decided' (util.rs 277-279), and the documented user flow reads the decided suffix and switches configuration only on StopSign(.., true) (reconfiguration.md 25-34). interpretations.rationale: Source reading of the re-synchronization path (PrepareReq -> Prepare -> Promise -> AcceptSync -> Accepted) suggests that a replica which has accepted the StopSign gets its accepted index inflated by one when it is re-synchronized at the same ballot: in handle_promise_accept the leader calls send_accsync, whose first branch uses the follower's own accepted index as the valid prefix (leader.rs 150-191), and that index already includes the StopSign because set_stopsign adds it (internal_storage.rs 503-512). create_log_sync then reports that index as LogSync.sync_idx with the sender's StopSign attached, and sync_log adds the StopSign once more, so the follower's accepted index ends at prefix + suffix + 1 while its decided index is the AcceptSync's decided index (internal_storage.rs 313-360). The follower then reports that inflated index in Accepted (follower.rs 112-126), and the leader's decision rule accepts any incoming accepted index whose count reaches a write quorum (leader.rs 316-345), so a write quorum of inflated reports would set the leader's decided index past the entries it holds. Both endpoints this reading endangers are public: is_reconfigured() is gated on stopsign_is_decided() (mod.rs 284-290, state_cache.rs 123-126), the bool of LogEntry::StopSign is documented as 'the reconfiguration has been decided' (util.rs 277-279), and the documented user flow reads the decided suffix and switches configuration only on StopSign(.., true) (reconfiguration.md 25-34). The final judgment is left unresolved until the two-case execution samples the endpoints; the reading also predicts that a fresh or lagging follower, whose prefix does not yet contain the StopSign, is unaffected. Counterevidence and limits: the reconfiguration documentation tells the user to start a new instance once the StopSign is observed as decided, so the affected window is an old instance that keeps running after (or while) it observes the decision and then re-synchronizes; the accounting is correct whenever sync_idx stays at or below the StopSign's own index, which covers the normal catch-up path; the account rests on static reading of the read() combination paths and of MemoryStorage's empty-range behaviour, not on an executed observation.

Confirmed by execution: the re-synchronization of a replica that already accepted its configuration's StopSign inflates its reported accepted index by one, and a write quorum of such reports makes the leader decide an index past every entry it holds. After both followers called reconnected(3): node 1 and node 2 reported accepted 7 over the same six indices of content, their read(5) returned None (the StopSign is now placed at index 6 by the internal index-type rule), and their decided-log read from 0 returned a single element (the StopSign), so the five decided entries disappeared from the readable decided log while is_reconfigured stayed true; node 3 (leader) reported decided 7 with accepted 6, is_reconfigured false where it had been true, read(5) = StopSign with decided = false, and read_decided_suffix(0) = None, i.e. the user on the leader can no longer read the decided log at all and never observes the reconfiguration as complete. interpretations.rationale: Source-only account of a lead, with an explicit argument for why it is not yet settled. trim takes its bound from the minimum of the recorded accepted indexes (util.rs 186-191) and compares the requested index against it (mod.rs 141-170), while the documented contract for trimming requires all nodes to have decided the trim index (compaction.md line 4); the parent question witnesses that those recorded indexes can exceed a replica's content by one per re-synchronization, so the minimum trim trusts is not necessarily a decided bound. The narrow counter-argument that keeps this unresolved rather than asserted: in the observed single-term drift the leading node's own recorded accepted index stayed at its content (6), so the minimum stayed truthful, and the trim bound is further adjusted by the StopSign (try_trim maps an index equal to the decided index to the decided log without the StopSign), which in the observed states cancelled the drift exactly. An over-trim therefore needs a state in which every recorded accepted index exceeds the entries its node holds, which the witnessed staleleader stage comes close to but was not sampled at a trim; the storage-side consequence I can source is that MemoryStorage computes suffix reads and prefix truncations by subtracting its compacted index (memory_storage.rs 64-67, 92-107, 122-127), so a compacted index above the requested prefix would underflow there.
counterevidence: In the observed drift the leading node's recorded accepted index stayed at its content, so the minimum trim uses was still truthful.
try_trim adjusts an index equal to the decided index to the decided log without the StopSign, which cancelled the observed drift instead of over-trimming.
limitations: No execution: trim after a drift was not exercised, and no observed state had every node's recorded accepted index above its content at the moment of a trim.
The underflow hypothesis rests on reading MemoryStorage's arithmetic; other storages may behave differently and the trait leaves out-of-range behaviour to the implementer.
The drift itself was exercised for three rounds only.
